newsitem.title: UK: EMU said to mean higher inflation, weaker bonds.
newsitem.headline: EMU said to mean higher inflation, weaker bonds.

text.p: Inflation will rise and bond markets will weaken in Europe under a single European currency, leading European analysts warned on Tuesday.

Prominent "Eurosceptic" and former European Commission official Bernard Connolly said at a bond conference in London the credit rating of indebted European government borrowers would worsen under European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), without the backing of explicit government guarantees.
This would put pressure on the supposedly independent nature of the European Central Bank (ECB), a cornerstone of EMU, Connolly said during a panel discussion on EMU.
"National governments will have a lot of influence over the ECB. The ECB will have to behave towards each Euro state in the way that a national central bank today does towards its own government.
"It will stand ready to create 'surprise' inflation to cut the real value of the governments' debt."

Connolly, author of leading Eurosceptic text "The Rotten Heart of Europe", which led to his departure from the European Commission's economic and monetary union unit in 1996, compared European governments under EMU with Canadian provinces.

"A 55 percent debt to GDP (gross domestic product) ratio appears to define the limit at which Canadian provinces can maintain investment grade status. What's going to make it possible for European governments to maintain good credit ratings with debt ratios significantly higher?" he said.
Governments and corporations which do not match up to the global rating agencies' investment grade criteria are classed as high risk, or "junk" borrowers.
European nations are striving to reach a debt to GDP ratio of 60 percent as one of the main criteria for joining EMU.

The current date for the first stage of EMU is January 1, 1999. But the failure of most member states of the European Union to come close to financial targets laid out in the Maastricht treaty is putting the timetable in doubt.
Tim Congdon, managing director of Lombard Street Research and one of the panel of "wise men", independent advisers to the British Treasury, also put himself in the Eurosceptic camp.
"EMU is not going to happen," he said. "I do not believe we can have monetary union without fiscal union."
Paul Mercier, head of financial markets at the European Monetary Institute in Frankfurt, the forerunner of the European Central Bank, defended the bank's independence.

"Some people know in advance how the ECB will behave. I do not know in advance how the ECB will behave. I can only guess. But I cannot imagine that when my bosses become governing members of the ECB they will suddenly behave in a totally crazy way."
Mercier dismissed comparisons between the ECB and the Reichsbank, which oversaw Germany's wild inflationary spiral during the ill-fated Weimar Republic of the 1920s.
"I am too young to remember the Reichsbank -- who cares about the Reichsbank?" he said.
